analysis.one_liner: Caps consumer loan interest rates at whatever cap the borrower's home state sets.
analysis.headline: The bill had only five original supporters, all Democrats or allied independents, and died in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing or a vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Truth in Lending Act so that no lender — including out-of-state and federally chartered lenders — could charge a consumer a higher annual percentage rate, fees included, than the consumer's own state allows. Today, nationally chartered banks can 'export' interest rates from states with no cap, and payday lenders use bank partnerships to sidestep state rate limits; this bill would override those escape routes with one sentence. It applied to all consumer credit except home mortgages.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers in states with interest rate caps — especially lower-income households who currently pay triple-digit annual rates on payday loans, auto title loans, and rent-a-bank installment loans. Consumers in states that cap rates would finally get those caps enforced against every lender, not just in-state ones.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers in states with rate caps

how_it_helps.text: The bill would bar any consumer credit transaction (except residential mortgages) from carrying an annual percentage rate above the maximum allowed in the borrower's home state, with fees counted toward the rate [S2][S3].

The provision applies 'notwithstanding any other provision of law,' which would override the federal rules that let nationally chartered banks lend at rates other states cap, closing the loophole payday lenders use through bank partnerships [S3].

analysis.who_pays: High-cost lenders whose business model depends on charging rates above state caps — payday lenders, auto title lenders, and banks or fintech companies that originate loans on their behalf — would lose revenue or lose that lending entirely. Some borrowers with poor credit could find fewer short-term credit options available.
analysis.who_pays_short: High-rate lenders and their bank partners

drawbacks.text: Strict rate caps can cut some borrowers with poor credit out of formal short-term credit entirely, leaving them with no options or pushing them toward unregulated lenders — a real cost that an honest supporter should acknowledge.
Because each state's own cap would control, states that set no limit would get no protection, and the patchwork could make multi-state lending more complicated for smaller lenders.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of borrowers paying triple-digit annual rates, the benefit is direct and large: their state's cap would finally apply to every lender. The tradeoff is real but narrower — some high-risk borrowers could lose access to quick cash — and states that want to offer such credit would still be free to set their own limits. On balance the bill shifts risk away from households and onto high-rate lenders.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read the bill twice and sent it to the Banking Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on April 3, 2019, joined by Sens. Jack Reed, Jeff Merkley, and Elizabeth Warren [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, which was the last action ever taken on it [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lenders that charge rates above state caps — payday lenders, auto title lenders, and the banks that partner with them — kept the status quo: no state cap applies to federally chartered loans, so the high-rate model continues unchanged. Households in rate-cap states remain exposed to the rent-a-bank loophole.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-rate lenders kept the status quo

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to apply each state's interest rate cap to all consumer lenders.

for.name: Sens. Jack Reed, Jeff Merkley, and Elizabeth Warren
for.role: Original cosponsors (Reed and Merkley D; Warren I)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors the day the bill was introduced.

against.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; the referral was the final action of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All five original supporters were Democrats plus one allied independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-chaired Banking Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: These lenders' core business is charging annual rates far above what most states allow — often 300% to 600%. Applying the borrower's home state cap to every loan, fees included, would remove the escape hatch they use to lend in capped states.

industries.industry: Banks and fintech partners in 'rent-a-bank' lending
industries.note: Some banks originate loans on behalf of high-rate lenders, then 'export' their national charter's rate to sidestep state caps and share the revenue. The bill's 'notwithstanding any other provision of law' language would end that arrangement, cutting off a fee stream for these banks.
